problem: VLM-based navigation policies such as NaVid, Uni-NaVid, NaVILA, StreamVLN and TrackVLA are each tied to one embodiment and camera setup, or to a narrow task family. Cross-task generalists assume a single fixed camera. Cross-embodiment generalists learn body priors implicitly but serve only one task, and they feed multi-view tokens to the model without explicit viewpoint or time cues. No single model covers VLN, object search, tracking and driving across wheeled, legged, aerial and car platforms with arbitrary camera rigs.
motivation: VLMs already generalise zero-shot across vision tasks, while embodied navigation remains fragmented by task, embodiment and instruction format. Almost every navigation task can be written as 'egocentric (multi-)camera video + language instruction → future trajectory'. Framed that way, one model can pool millions of heterogeneous samples (simulator VLN, ObjectNav, tracking, UAV, driving, web video) and co-train them with image/video QA, as long as tokens from different cameras and timesteps can be told apart and the token count stays within a deployment budget.
key_idea: Train one video-VLM (NavFoM) on 8.02M cross-embodiment, cross-task navigation samples plus 4.76M QA samples. It uses Temporal-Viewpoint Indicator (TVI) tokens to label each frame's camera azimuth and timestep, and Budget-Aware Temporal Sampling (BATS) to keep history within a fixed token budget; an MLP head regresses normalized waypoint trajectories.
insight: Explicit, separate indicator tokens work better than injecting view/time information into the visual tokens. On RxR-CE four-view, TVI tokens reach 64.4 SR, versus 52.3 for HAMT-style viewpoint-history positional embeddings added to visual tokens, 59.1 for per-view learned special tokens, and 53.6 for handcrafted sinusoidal tokens without MLP projectors. The authors argue this is because TVI tokens do not disturb the pretrained visual token space. BATS, a forgetting-curve sampler that keeps recent frames densely and old frames sparsely, beats uniform sampling (62.4), linear-probability sampling (63.0) and token merging (63.2) at B=2048. At B=1024 its nDTW drops only 1.7 points (65.8→64.1), versus 6.0 for uniform and 5.9 for linear sampling, measured against BATS at B=2048; the paper prints these drops as 1.4/6.0/5.2. Cross-task co-training matters most where the task's own data mismatch the evaluation: four-view Searching rises from 10.3 to 45.2 SR and four-view Tracking from 12.6 to 62.0 SR once other tasks' multi-view, open-set data are added. More cameras help VLN up to four (+5.5 SR on R2R-CE, +7.0 on RxR-CE versus single view), but six cameras slightly hurt under a fixed budget because history tokens get crowded out.
method: Unified task formulation: given an instruction L and RGB video from N cameras over T steps, predict 8 waypoints a=(x,y,z,θ). z is used only for UAVs; waypoints are normalized to [-1,1] by per-embodiment scale factors (indoor 1.0 m / UAV 7.93 m / car 50.8 m in x, set at the 99th percentile).

Observation encoding: DINOv2 and SigLIP features (576 patches) are concatenated channel-wise and grid-average-pooled to 64 tokens (fine: current frame, image QA) or 4 tokens (coarse: history, video QA), then projected into the LLM (Qwen2-7B) by a 2-layer MLP.

Temporal-Viewpoint Indicator (TVI) tokens: one indicator token per frame, E_Base + MLP(sinusoidal TimePE(t)) + MLP(sinusoidal PE of cos/sin of azimuth φ) for navigation. Video QA uses base+time only and image QA uses base only, which lets arbitrary camera rigs and QA data share one token layout.

Budget-Aware Temporal Sampling (BATS): once tokens exceed budget B, each history frame is kept with probability P(t)=(1-ε)e^{k(t-T)/T}+ε with ε=0.1. k is solved offline with Brent's method so that the expected tokens ((4+1)E_frames+(64+1))N ≤ B. If still over budget, the oldest frames are dropped. This gives near-constant inference time across the episode.

Dual-branch heads and loss: a language-model head handles QA with cross-entropy; a 3-layer MLP planning head maps the action hidden state to the trajectory with MSE on valid dimensions. Total loss is L = 10·L_nav + L_QA; one epoch on 56 H100 × 72 h, with cached coarse visual features (2.9× faster training, 1.8× less memory).

Data and action unification: Habitat discrete actions are converted into trajectories built from atomic 12.5 cm forward / 15° turn steps. VLN, tracking and UAV data use camera randomization (1–8 surrounding views, height 0.6–1.5 m, HFoV 75–120°). At VLN-CE evaluation the discrete actions are replaced by predicted-trajectory execution.

Real-world deployment: the model runs on a remote GPU server (≤0.5 s per 8-waypoint trajectory at a 1600-token budget) and robots stream compressed observations asynchronously. Each platform's own local planner (possibly LiDAR-based) tracks the predicted trajectory.

setting.backbone: Qwen2-7B LLM with DINOv2 + SigLIP vision encoders, 2-layer MLP projector, MLP planning head (fine-tuned end-to-end from pretrained weights)
setting.training_data: 12.7M samples, 1 epoch. 8.02M navigation samples: VLN 3.37M (VLN-CE R2R/RxR 2.94M recorded along GT paths with randomized multi-camera rigs; OpenUAV/TravelUAV 429K with 4 views); ObjectNav 1.02M (successful L3MVN episodes on HM3D ObjectNav, single view); active visual tracking 897K (EVT-Bench); driving 681K (nuScenes 27K + OpenScene 654K); Sekai web-video navigation 2.03M (~182K YouTube videos, VLM-generated instructions, SLAM trajectories). Plus 3.15M image-QA and 1.61M video-QA samples.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB video from a variable number of cameras (1, 4, 6 or 8 views) + language instruction; no depth, no odometry
setting.action_space: predicted trajectory of 8 waypoints (x, y, [z], yaw), normalized per embodiment; replaces Habitat discrete actions at evaluation; real robots track it with their own local planners
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE R2R/RxR, HM3D-OVON, EVT-Bench); OpenUAV/TravelUAV simulator; NAVSIM pseudo-simulation; nuScenes open-loop
setting.privileged: none (RGB + instruction only); in the real world, platform-specific local planners may use LiDAR to follow predicted trajectories

results: A single checkpoint with no task-specific fine-tuning sets the reported state of the art on VLN-CE. Four-view RGB reaches R2R-CE 61.7 SR / 55.3 SPL and RxR-CE 64.4 SR versus HNR's 56.3, which uses RGB-D and odometry. Single-view reaches R2R-CE 56.2 SR and RxR-CE 57.4 SR versus StreamVLN-RGB's 55.7 and 51.8. Zero-shot on HM3D-OVON val-unseen it gets 45.2 SR / 31.9 SPL, beating MTU3D (40.8 SR) and Uni-NaVid (39.5 SR). It also beats TravelUAV on all OpenUAV splits (e.g. 29.83 vs 22.42 SR on unseen-object) and TrackVLA on EVT-Bench (distracted 62.0 vs 57.6 SR), while only matching driving specialists: NAVSIM PDMS 84.3 vs DiffusionDrive 88.1, nuScenes avg L2 0.42 vs EMMA 0.32.
limitations: Evaluation is not strictly comparable to standard VLN-CE and Habitat protocols: discrete actions are replaced by trajectory-based execution. Several training sources overlap the benchmark domains (OpenScene with NAVSIM, EVT-Bench, TravelUAV). Real-world results are reported only in figures, on 110 hand-designed cases in a 5 m × 5 m area.

Performance collapses on OpenUAV Unseen-Map (6.30 SR), attributed to limited UAV data and exploration ability. Driving remains below specialised planners, and the model has no explicit lane or agent modelling.

A fixed token budget trades views against history: six cameras underperform four. Four-view gains on tracking are small (+0.6 SR on Distracted Target) because EVT-Bench targets spawn in front of the robot. No downward-facing UAV camera is used.
